name: Semmelweis reflex
statement: The reflex-like rejection of new evidence because it contradicts an established belief, named for the Vienna obstetrician whose handwashing results his colleagues dismissed.
meaning: The name asserts a mechanism rather than an outcome. It says the evidence is refused because of the conflict, before it is weighed, and Robert Anton Wilson's original definition went further and had the group punish the discoverer. Testing that would mean showing the same evidence judged worse when it cuts against a held position, and judged that way without engagement. Three separate things travel under the name and pull apart on inspection: a real episode in Vienna between 1846 and 1861, a retelling of it that has the numbers and the reception wrong, and a phrase coined in 1979 that never became a research programme.

origin.where: The Game of Life, by Timothy Leary
origin.note: The definition sits in a footnote on page 43 and is presented as an entry from a fictional reference work, 'Webster's Galactic Dictionary, 23rd Edition': 'Mob behavior found among primates and larval hominids on undeveloped planets, in which a discovery of important scientific fact is punished rather than rewarded.' The book is a treatment of the Tarot as a map of evolution. Its title page credits Leary as author and Wilson with its historical and scholarly scripts, and the copyright page goes further: it lists the pages Wilson wrote, and page 43 is among them. That line, not the general credit, is why the definition is Wilson's. The copy read for this entry is the 1993 New Falcon printing, copyright 1979.

evidence: Semmelweis was appointed in 1846 to the Vienna Maternity Hospital, which ran two clinics. The first taught doctors and medical students, the second trained midwives, and women were admitted on alternate days with no clinical selection. Loudon calls that a controlled trial by accident rather than design. From 1840 through 1846 the two clinics recorded 42,795 births and 2,977 maternal deaths. Over those years mortality ran at 98.4 per 1,000 births in the first clinic against 36.2 per 1,000 in the second. Loudon gives that pair in his own text and cites his two books for it, not the treatise. In May 1847 Semmelweis required students to wash in chloride of lime before entering the first clinic. In 1848 the first clinic recorded 12.7 maternal deaths per 1,000 births, against 13.3 in the second. Table XXIV of Semmelweis's treatise is the source of a different and longer series, which Loudon reprints for 1784 to 1859 and which this entry uses only for the period rates. La Rochelle and Julien used the monthly series instead. Average monthly mortality was 10.65% from January 1841 to May 1847 and 1.98% from the introduction of handwashing to February 1849, a risk ratio of 5.38. Their interrupted time-series model put the handwashing coefficient at -0.0887 with a standard error of 0.0310, p = 0.0042, which they describe as an absolute reduction of 8.87% and as one death avoided for every eleven women examined. Semmelweis held that childbed fever was caused by decaying animal-organic matter absorbed through the placental bed or through injuries sustained in delivery. Bacteria had no part in it. Pasteur's work was still a decade off.

replication.headline: No study measuring the Semmelweis reflex as named was found; the two nearest measured things are an 8.6% rise in outside publications after an eminent scientist dies, and 2,034 citations to papers that had already been retracted.
replication.detail: Azoulay, Fons-Rosen and Graff Zivin tracked entry into the subfields of 452 star life scientists who died while still active. Publications by the star's previous collaborators fell 20.7%. Publications by non-collaborators rose 8.6%, the effect grew monotonically with citation impact, and the growth was mostly carried by articles that do not build on the star's own work. What the authors rule out is the crude version of gatekeeping. In the five years before death only three of the 452 sat on NIH study sections and only three were journal editors, so the stars were not controlling funding or journals. They favour what they call Goliath's shadow, outsiders deterred by the prospect of challenging a luminary, and they read their result as consistent with Planck rather than against him. Deterred entry is not the refusal of evidence the reflex describes. These figures were read from the NIH author manuscript of the published article, deposited as NIHMS1055244, which carries each of them; an earlier version of this entry took them from the NBER working paper and said no published copy had been opened. The other measured neighbour runs in the opposite direction. Budd, Sievert and Schultz searched MEDLINE from 1966 through August 1997, identified 235 retracted articles and counted 2,034 citations to them after the retraction notice. Of 299 citations examined, 19 noted the retraction and 280 treated the article as valid, 17 explicitly and 263 by implication. That is discredited work surviving, rather than sound work being refused. Neither literature is the operationalised one. For evidence that survives correction, see entries 187 and 192.

limits: The reflex has never been operationalised. A Europe PMC search for the phrase on 21 September 2026 returned 32 records, the earliest from 2009, and not one measures the thing the name asserts. Most are editorials, historical pieces, narrative reviews or commentaries. Six are typed as research articles, but those are empirical studies in other fields, on abdominal binders and on lunar phase and suicide among them, which invoke the phrase in passing. A Crossref search the same day returned book chapters, opinion articles and biographical notes of the same character. Searches covered Europe PMC, Crossref, the DataCite and Crossref DOI records for every citation here, Google Books, the Internet Archive and the open web. The historical record is itself contested. Tulodziecki argues that Semmelweis was not the excellent reasoner he is assumed to be, and that the puzzle of his rejection dissolves once that is admitted. Kadar and Croft answer that her account of his theory has no basis in fact and rests on Loudon's misrepresentation of what happened after May 1847. Loudon, who is hostile to the hagiography, still calls the observations original and astute, and separately notes that Semmelweis was intolerant of criticism to the point of paranoia and that his treatise mixes clarity with muddled and bellicose attacks on his critics. Nothing in the sources read here settles which account of the rejection is right.
misreadings: The famous figures are wrong. The fall from 18% to 2.45% comes from Hebra's editorial of December 1847, which set two unrepresentative averages beside each other. April and May 1847 gave 17.2%, or 96 deaths in 558 women, and were taken to stand for the period before handwashing, although January, February and March of the same year had run at 3.21%, 1.02% and 3.6%. Wieger's annual rate for the first clinic in 1848 was 1.27%, from 45 deaths, against annual death counts of 238 to 521 in the years before. The improvement also did not hold at the 1848 level. Table XXIV of the treatise, as Loudon reprints it, has the first clinic running at 35.7 deaths per 1,000 births across 1848 to 1859 and the second at 30.6. The same table gives 90.2 and 33.8 for the two clinics across 1839 to 1847, so the better known 98.4 and 36.2 are a narrower seven-year figure from Loudon's text and not the table's. The silence is a myth too. Hebra announced the discovery in print in December 1847 and asked other institutions for confirming or disconfirming results, Wieger published the actual figures in the Gazette medicale de Strasbourg on 20 April 1849, Skoda described the work to the Imperial Academy of Sciences on 18 October 1849, and Semmelweis gave his own first public account to the Society of Physicians on 15 May 1850. His treatise, dated 1861, appeared in 1860, thirteen years after the intervention. What the record shows is not refusal to look but a specific objection to the inference. An editorial in the Gazette medicale de Paris in 1850 granted the fall and denied that it followed from the washing, since epidemics of puerperal fever were known to fluctuate and the rate might have dropped for another reason. Kadar and Croft argue from Lesky's archive documents that Semmelweis's chief, Johann Klein, refused the evidence on that same ground. They argue separately, from Kadar's own work on the animal experiments, that Semmelweis ran his rabbit trials to answer it. Post hoc is not propter hoc, and the men who said so were right about the logic even though they were wrong about the world. Antisepsis reached obstetrics in the 1880s through Lister, who had not heard of Semmelweis until his own method was established. Wilson's glossary entry, finally, describes puerperal fever as a now-obsolete disease.

sources.text: Loudon, I. (2013). Ignaz Phillip Semmelweis' studies of death in childbirth. Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, 106(11), 461-463. Read in full on 21 September 2026 in the James Lind Library commentary that the JRSM article republishes, at jameslindlibrary.org. Loudon's reprint of Table XXIV is the source of the period rates used here; Semmelweis's treatise itself was not consulted directly, and the 98.4 and 36.2 per 1,000 figures are from Loudon's own text rather than from that table.

La Rochelle, P., & Julien, A.-S. (2013). How dramatic were the effects of handwashing on maternal mortality observed by Ignaz Semmelweis? Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, 106(11), 459-460. Read in full on 21 September 2026 in the James Lind Library commentary the JRSM article republishes; every figure quoted here was checked against its table and text.

Kadar, N., & Croft, R. D. (2020). Why Semmelweis's doctrine was rejected: evidence from the first publication of his results by Friedrich Wieger, and an editorial commenting on the results. The British Journal for the History of Science, 53(3), 389-395. Open access; the seven-page PDF was downloaded from Cambridge Core and read in full on 21 September 2026, after a first request returned a 502.

Tulodziecki, D. (2013). Shattering the myth of Semmelweis. Philosophy of Science, 80(5), 1065-1075. The full text is behind Cambridge Core's paywall and was not obtained on 21 September 2026: the PDF route answered 200 with the article landing page, which itself carried a notice of a temporary service suspension, and Unpaywall, OpenAIRE and Semantic Scholar all record no open copy. The publisher's own abstract on that landing page was read, together with Kadar and Croft's account of the argument.

Leary, T. (1979/1993). The Game of Life. Phoenix: New Falcon Publications, p. 43. Historical and scholarly scripts by Robert Anton Wilson, and page 43 is named on the copyright page as one Wilson wrote. The source of the phrase; the Internet Archive scan of the 1993 printing was downloaded and read on 21 September 2026.

Azoulay, P., Fons-Rosen, C., & Graff Zivin, J. S. (2019). Does science advance one funeral at a time? American Economic Review, 109(8), 2889-2920. The publisher's own PDF is closed, but the NIH author manuscript of this article (NIHMS1055244, PMC6814193) was downloaded from the PubMed Central REST route on 21 September 2026 and carries every figure quoted here.

Azoulay, P., Fons-Rosen, C., & Graff Zivin, J. S. (2015, revised 2018). Does science advance one funeral at a time? NBER Working Paper 21788. The preprint, downloaded and kept for comparison. The figures in this entry are now taken from the author manuscript of the published article rather than from this version.

Budd, J. M., Sievert, M., & Schultz, T. R. (1998). Phenomena of retraction: reasons for retraction and citations to the publications. JAMA, 280(3), 296-297. The JAMA page answered a Cloudflare interstitial rather than a paywall on 21 September 2026, and the Wayback Machine's replay died on the egress tunnel across eleven attempts the same day. Every figure used here appears in the structured MEDLINE abstract, which was fetched from the PubMed REST route and read.

Gupta, V. K., Saini, C., Oberoi, M., Kalra, G., & Nasir, M. I. (2020). Semmelweis reflex: an age-old prejudice. World Neurosurgery, 136, e119-e125. A narrative review, cited here as an example of how the term is used in the medical literature. The Elsevier full text is closed and was not obtained; the structured abstract was read from PubMed on 21 September 2026, and it describes a keyword search with no measurement.
